commitResults.messageTitle: Level-0: Rename to saLLMan, add greeting and exit
commitResults.messageBody:
Rename the chatbot from the placeholder Duke to saLLMan, replacing the
banner with matching ASCII art and updating the docs. The bot now greets
the user and exits.

commitResults.messageTitle: Level-1: Echo user input until bye
commitResults.messageBody:
Read commands in a loop and echo them back, exiting on bye. Extract a
say() helper since every reply now shares the same divider formatting.

commitResults.messageTitle: Level-2: Store and list tasks
commitResults.messageBody:
Keep entered text in a fixed-size array and print it numbered on the list
command, per the <=100 task assumption. Other input is stored rather than
echoed.

commitResults.messageTitle: Level-3: Mark tasks as done
commitResults.messageBody:
Track completion in a boolean array parallel to the task descriptions and
add a mark command. Extract formatTask() so list and mark share one status
format.

commitResults.messageTitle: Level-3: Reverse done status with unmark
commitResults.messageBody:
Add an unmark command mirroring mark, so a task wrongly marked done can be
set back to not done.

commitResults.messageTitle: Level-3: Extract a Task class (A-Classes)
commitResults.messageBody:
Replace the parallel description/status arrays with a Task object owning
both, moving status formatting into Task.toString(). Fields are protected
so Level-4 task types can inherit them.

commitResults.messageTitle: Level-4: Add todos, deadlines and events (A-Inheritance)
commitResults.messageBody:
Introduce Todo, Deadline and Event subclasses of Task, each overriding
toString() to add its type icon and any date fields. Dates stay free text
for now. Unknown input no longer creates an untyped task.

commitResults.messageTitle: Level-5: Handle the two basic input errors (minimal)
commitResults.messageBody:
Report a todo with no description and an unrecognised command instead of
mishandling them. Match a bare todo in its own branch so the missing
description is named rather than reported as an unknown command.

commitResults.messageTitle: Level-5: Handle all current error cases (typical)
commitResults.messageBody:
Split each input into command and arguments before dispatching, so a command
given without arguments reaches its own branch and can name what is missing.
Validate task numbers, deadline and event parts, and the full-list case.
Split on the bare /by and /from tokens so a missing description is diagnosed
correctly rather than reported as a missing delimiter.

commitResults.messageTitle: Level-5: Make error messages specific and actionable (stretch)
commitResults.messageBody:
Split the generic deadline and event errors into one message per failure, each
naming the missing part and pairing it with a worked example. Report the valid
task number range, and give an empty list its own message rather than telling
the user to pick from 1 to 0.

commitResults.messageTitle: Level-5: Introduce SallmanException (A-Exceptions)
commitResults.messageBody:
Replace the say-and-continue error blocks with a checked SallmanException
thrown from four validating parse methods and caught once in the main loop.
NumberFormatException is translated into a message phrased for the user.
Behaviour is unchanged; all 13 UI test cases still pass.

commitResults.messageTitle: Level-6: Store tasks in an ArrayList (A-Collections)
commitResults.messageBody:
Replace the fixed-size array and its separate taskCount with a List, so
remove() closes the gap and size() is always in step with the contents. Drops
the 100-task limit and its full-list error.

commitResults.messageTitle: A-Enums: Represent commands as an enum
commitResults.messageBody:
Replace the chain of string comparisons with a Command enum and a switch, so
an unknown keyword is rejected once in fromKeyword() and every case is a known
command. The help text is now built from the constants, which stops it drifting
from the actual command set as it did when delete was added.

commitResults.messageTitle: Level-7: Save tasks to disk and reload on startup
commitResults.messageBody:
The task list only existed in memory, so everything was lost when the
chatbot exited.

Add a Storage class that writes the list to a text file whenever it
changes and reads it back at startup. Each task renders itself via a
toFileFormat() method, mirroring how toString() already works, so the
subclasses stay responsible for their own fields.

The path is built with java.nio.file.Path so it works on any OS, and is
relative so the app is not tied to one computer. A missing data file
means a first run rather than an error, and the containing folder is
created on demand.

The data file path can be overridden by a command line argument. Without
it the UI tests would share, and overwrite, the real task list.

commitResults.messageTitle: Level-7: Survive a corrupted save file
commitResults.messageBody:
The loader trusted the data file completely, so a single damaged line
crashed the chatbot on startup with a stack trace and made every other
saved task unreachable. The file is plain text and invites hand editing,
so this is a realistic way to lose a task list.

Validate each line and skip only the ones that fail, keeping the rest.
Each rejection names the line number and the specific fault, so a
hand-edited file can be corrected rather than guessed at. Blank lines are
ignored silently, since a trailing newline is normal.

Checking the fields separately, rather than catching whatever exception
the parsing happens to throw, is what makes those specific messages
possible.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-Level-7'
commitResults.messageBody:
Add task persistence: the list is saved to a text file whenever it
changes, reloaded at startup, and a corrupted save file is repaired
rather than fatal.

commitResults.messageTitle: Level-8: Parse dates instead of storing them as text
commitResults.messageBody:
Deadline and event dates were kept as whatever the user typed, so the
chatbot could not compare or reformat them, and "Sunday" was as valid as
a real date.

Store them as java.time.LocalDate. Dates are entered as yyyy-mm-dd and
shown back as MMM dd yyyy, e.g. 2019-10-15 is displayed as Oct 15 2019.
Both conversions live in a TaskDate helper so the two formats are defined
once rather than once per task type.

The data file keeps the input format rather than the display format, so
saved dates can be read back regardless of how they are shown.

This makes the chatbot stricter: text that is not a date is now refused,
where before it was accepted verbatim. That is the point of the
increment, but it does mean an existing data file with free-text dates
will have those lines reported as unreadable on the next start.

commitResults.messageTitle: Level-8: Add an on command to list tasks by date
commitResults.messageBody:
Storing real dates made it possible to ask questions about them, but
nothing did. Finding what is happening on a particular day meant reading
the whole list by eye.

Add "on <date>", which lists the deadlines due that day and the events
running over it. Each task type answers for itself through an isOn
method: a plain task is never on a date, a deadline matches its due
date, and an event matches any day it spans, not only its start and end.
Putting the test on the task rather than in the command keeps the
command from having to know which subclass it is looking at.

A date with nothing on it says so, rather than printing a heading with
nothing under it.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-Level-8'
commitResults.messageBody:
Give tasks real dates: deadlines and events now hold a LocalDate parsed
from yyyy-mm-dd and displayed as MMM dd yyyy, and an on command lists
whatever falls on a given day.

commitResults.messageTitle: Storage: Keep descriptions containing the field separator
commitResults.messageBody:
The data file separates fields with " | " and the loader split each line
on every occurrence, so a description containing that sequence broke the
round trip. A todo was silently truncated at the first occurrence, losing
text without any warning, and a deadline or event was rejected on the
next load, losing the whole task.

The description is the only free-text field and the dates that follow it
never contain the separator, so split the type and done flag off the
front and the dates off the back, leaving whatever remains as the
description. That is unambiguous regardless of what the description
contains.

The complaint about a saved line like "T | 0 | " changes from a field
count to naming the empty description, which is what is actually wrong
with it.

commitResults.messageTitle: Level-8: Reject an event that ends before it starts
commitResults.messageBody:
Nothing checked the order of the two dates, so "event x /from 2019-10-20
/to 2019-10-10" was accepted. Such an event spans no days, so the on
command could never find it, and the list showed a range that reads as
nonsense. Getting the two dates the wrong way round is an easy typo.

Refuse it at the point the event is built, and say which part to check.
A same-day event is still allowed, since a start equal to the end is a
legitimate one-day event rather than a mistake.

commitResults.messageTitle: A-MoreOOP: Extract a TaskList class
commitResults.messageBody:
The task list was a bare List<Task> held in main, so every operation on
it was spelled out at the call site and the loop that searches by date
sat in the same class as the console output.

Move the list and the operations over it into a TaskList class. Callers
now ask the list for what they need rather than iterating it themselves,
and tasksOn() lives next to the data it searches.

TaskList deals only in 0-based positions. Converting from the 1-based
numbers shown to the user stays with the code that reads the input,
so there is one place where that conversion happens.

commitResults.messageTitle: A-MoreOOP: Extract a Ui class and build the app as an object
commitResults.messageBody:
Reading input, printing replies and deciding what to do all sat together
in one static main, so the wording of every message was interleaved with
the logic that produced it.

Move the console in and out into a Ui class, and turn Sallman into an
object holding a Ui, a Storage and a TaskList, with a run() loop over
them. The rest of the app now reports what happened and lets Ui decide
how to say it, which is also what would have to change first to give the
chatbot a different kind of interface.

Loading now happens in the constructor. A data file that cannot be read
leaves the chatbot usable with an empty list rather than stopping it
from starting.

commitResults.messageTitle: A-MoreOOP: Extract a Parser class
commitResults.messageBody:
Turning text into commands, task numbers, dates and tasks was spread
through the main class alongside the code that acted on the results, so
Sallman had to know the shape of every command as well as what to do
with it.

Move that work into a Parser. Sallman now asks for a command and a task
and acts on what comes back, without handling raw text itself. The
worked examples used in the error hints move with it, since they
describe the input formats Parser is the one enforcing.

Sallman drops from 302 lines to 159, and the four classes the increment
asks for -- Ui, Storage, Parser, TaskList -- now each hold one concern.

commitResults.messageTitle: A-MoreOOP: Turn commands into objects
commitResults.messageBody:
The main loop held a switch over every command, so it knew both which
commands exist and what each one does. Every new command meant another
branch in the same method.

Rename the enum to CommandType, which is what it always was: the table
mapping typed keywords to known command words. Command is now an
abstract class, with a subclass per command that carries itself out
through execute(tasks, ui, storage). The loop asks Parser for a Command
and runs it without knowing which one it holds, and ends when the
command says so through isExit().

Task numbers are checked when a command runs rather than while parsing,
because whether a number is in range depends on the list, which the
parser does not see. Parsing checks the wording, execution checks it
against the state.

Sallman drops from 159 lines to 85, and its run() is now the loop and
nothing else.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-MoreOOP'
commitResults.messageBody:
Split the chatbot into Ui, Storage, Parser and TaskList, and give each
command its own class so the main loop runs any command without knowing
which one it holds.

commitResults.messageTitle: A-Packages: Move the classes into a sallman package
commitResults.messageBody:
All nineteen classes sat in the default package, which gives them no
namespace of their own and is not something a real project would ship.

Put them in a package named after the chatbot, keeping src/main/java as
the source root so the tools used later still find the sources where
they expect them.

The run command gains the package folder, so the README and the UI test
runner are updated to match.

commitResults.messageTitle: A-Packages: Split into sallman.task and sallman.command
commitResults.messageBody:
One package of nineteen classes said nothing about how they relate.
Three of them are the app's plumbing, five describe what a task is, and
eight describe what the user can ask for.

Split the task types into sallman.task and the command objects into
sallman.command, leaving the parts that wire the app together in
sallman. The imports now state which parts depend on which, and where a
new class belongs is decided by what it is rather than by where there
is room.

The dependencies run one way: sallman.task imports nothing else from the
app, sallman.command builds on both, and sallman holds the loop. Nothing
imports in the opposite direction, so the task types can be reasoned
about without reading the rest.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-Packages'
commitResults.messageBody:
Organise the classes into sallman, sallman.task and sallman.command, with
src/main/java kept as the source root.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'add-gradle-support'
A-Gradle: Point the Gradle build at this project
commitResults.messageBody:
The build file merged from add-gradle-support still names the template's
main class and JAR, so the application and shadowJar tasks would have
failed on this project.

Set mainClass to sallman.Sallman and name the shadow JAR after the
chatbot. No other change is needed: the build already expects sources
under src/main/java, which is where A-Packages left them, and already
declares the JUnit and shadow plugins that the next two increments use.

commitResults.messageTitle: A-Gradle: Enable assertions and document the Gradle workflow
commitResults.messageBody:
Following the Gradle tutorial's remaining steps now that the build file
points at this project.

Turn on assertions for the run task. Java ignores assertions unless
asked to check them, so without this a failing assertion would pass
silently and there would be little point writing any.

Rewrite the README around Gradle. Its setup steps still described
opening the project as a plain Java one and running the main class by
right-clicking it, and the sample output it promised was the greeting
from Level-0, which the chatbot stopped printing several increments ago.
It now covers importing as a Gradle project, the tasks worth knowing,
the commands the chatbot accepts, and where the task list is saved.

commitResults.messageTitle: A-JUnit: Add JUnit tests for the logic classes
commitResults.messageBody:
The only automated checks were the text-UI tests, which drive the whole
program through its console. They catch a broken feature but point at a
transcript rather than a method, and they cannot reach cases the console
cannot produce.

Add JUnit tests for the five classes that hold logic worth testing:
Parser, Storage, TaskList, TaskDate and the task types. They cover the
boundaries most likely to be wrong -- the ends of a task-number range,
dates that look valid but are not, and the days an event spans -- and
assert the specific message for each rejection, so a wrong-but-plausible
error is a failure rather than a pass.

Storage is tested against a JUnit temporary folder, so a test run can
never read or overwrite the real task list.

53 tests. Checked they fail when they should by breaking Event.isOn to
match only an event's end points: two tests failed, naming the method.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-JUnit'
commitResults.messageBody:
Add JUnit tests for Parser, Storage, TaskList, TaskDate and the task
types, covering the boundaries most likely to be wrong and asserting the
specific message for each rejection.

commitResults.messageTitle: Level-9: Add a find command
commitResults.messageBody:
There was no way to pick out a task without reading the whole list,
which stops being practical once the list is long.

Add "find <keyword>", listing the tasks whose description contains it.
Matching ignores case, since remembering the exact capitalisation of a
task defeats the point of searching for it.

Each task answers for itself through hasKeyword, the same way isOn
already works, so the search does not need to know how a description is
stored. Only the description is searched: a deadline's date is shown to
the user but is not part of what the task is about.

commitResults.messageTitle: A-JavaDoc: Document the command classes and the packages
commitResults.messageBody:
Every public method already carried a header comment except the
execute() overrides, which inherited theirs from the abstract Command.
Inherited text says what a command does in general, not what each one
does in particular, and says nothing about which of them save the list
or what each can throw.

Give every execute() and isExit() its own header. Add package-info files
for the three packages, describing what each is for and, for
sallman.task, that it depends on nothing else in the app.

commitResults.messageTitle: A-CodingStandard: Comply with the SE-EDU Java standard
commitResults.messageBody:
Auditing the code against the standard found one kind of violation: the
tests named LocalDate and ArrayList in full at the point of use instead
of importing them, where the standard asks for classes to be imported
explicitly. Everything else already complied, including the rules that
are easy to trip over: no wildcard imports, American spelling, and
abbreviations not written in uppercase inside a name.

Record the standard in AGENTS.md, along with the Git commit convention
that also applies from this week. The increment asks for new code to keep
complying, and a rule written down where the next change will be made is
more likely to be followed than one that has to be remembered.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-JavaDoc'
commitResults.messageBody:
Give every execute() and isExit() its own header comment, and add
package-info files for the three packages.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-CodingStandard'
commitResults.messageBody:
Import LocalDate and ArrayList explicitly in the tests, and record the
Java and Git standards in AGENTS.md.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-Level-9'
commitResults.messageBody:
Add a find command that lists tasks whose description contains a
keyword.

commitResults.messageTitle: Document FindCommand to match the other commands
commitResults.messageBody:
A-JavaDoc gave every command's execute() its own header comment, and
Level-9 added FindCommand. Both branches started from the same commit,
so neither could see the other: FindCommand did not exist when the
headers were written, and the headers did not exist when it was.

Git merged both without complaint because they touched different files.
The result still compiled and passed every test while being the one
command documented differently from the rest, which is the kind of gap a
textual merge cannot notice.

commitResults.messageTitle: A-CheckStyle: Enforce the coding standard with Checkstyle
commitResults.messageBody:
The standard was written down in AGENTS.md during A-CodingStandard, but
nothing checked it. Following a written rule depends on remembering it,
and the violations this found were exactly the kind nobody notices by
eye.

Add the Checkstyle plugin with the configuration AddressBook Level 3
uses, so the rules being enforced are the ones the course teaches rather
than a set invented here.

It reported 28 violations, in three groups:

Ten were switch case labels indented level with the switch rather than
one step deeper. The config sets caseIndent=4, so the indented form is
the one this course expects.

Two were declaration order in TaskDate: public constants declared after
a private one. Public members come first, so a reader meets the class's
interface before its internals.

Sixteen were a line break placing an opening parenthesis at the start of
a continuation line, all in the tests. Most were fixed by joining the
call onto one line. The five that would not fit shared the same shape,
so they became a helper method, which reads better than the original.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-CheckStyle'
commitResults.messageBody:
Add Checkstyle with the AddressBook Level 3 configuration and fix the 28
violations it reported.

commitResults.messageTitle: Level-10: Add a JavaFX GUI
commitResults.messageBody:
The chatbot could only be used from a terminal.

Add a JavaFX window: the conversation in a scrolling pane, an input box
and a Send button, with each speaker's messages on their own side. The
layout is FXML and the styling CSS, both carried over from the tutorial
project, so the design lives outside the Java code.

Keep the text interface working as well. The two front ends share one
path: Ui collects what it says, the console prints it as it goes, and the
GUI asks for the text once the command is finished. Keeping it means the
26 text-UI test cases still guard the logic, which a GUI is much harder
to subject to automated tests.

Launcher exists only to start the application without itself extending
Application, which trips a classpath check when run from a JAR.

Replies are coloured by the kind of command that produced them, so adding
a task looks different from deleting one before the text is read. An exit
command leaves its goodbye on screen for a moment so it can be read
before the window closes.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-Level-10'
commitResults.messageBody:
Add a JavaFX GUI while keeping the text interface, both driven through the
same Ui so the text-UI tests still guard the logic.

commitResults.messageTitle: A-Varargs: Take exception hints as varargs
commitResults.messageBody:
SallmanException had two constructors differing only in whether a hint
followed the message, and could carry at most one. Advice needing two
lines had to be squeezed into one string or split across the message.

Take the hints as varargs instead. One constructor now covers a bare
message, a message with an example, and a message needing several lines,
and every existing call site compiles unchanged.

Also collapse three identical blocks in Ui that each built a heading
followed by numbered tasks, for the full list, search results and one
day's tasks. They now share sayNumbered, which gathers the lines and
hands them to say() as its varargs argument. That is what lets one reply
hold a heading and however many tasks there happen to be.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-Varargs'
commitResults.messageBody:
Take exception hints as varargs, and share one numbered-list helper across
the three places that built one.

commitResults.messageTitle: Document how to run the released JAR
commitResults.messageBody:
The README explains how to build and run saLLMan from source, but says
nothing about the JAR published on the releases page. A user who only
wants to use the chatbot has to either clone the repository and set up
Gradle, or find the release themselves and guess what to do with the
file they downloaded.

The opening line also describes saLLMan as a command-line chatbot, which
stopped being accurate when the JavaFX window was added in Level-10.

Let's add a section near the top that points at the latest release and
gives the command to run the JAR, and drop "command-line" from the
opening line.

The section links to /releases/latest rather than to a fixed version, so
that it stays correct as later releases are published. It also mentions
that JavaFX is bundled and that the save file is written next to the
JAR, because both of those surprise a first-time user.

commitResults.messageTitle: A-Assertions: Assert the assumptions the code relies on
commitResults.messageBody:
Several methods depend on guarantees that are established somewhere
else. TaskList.get and TaskList.remove index the list directly, because
the parser has already rejected a task number outside it. Storage
reads exactly three fields from a saved line after checking that there
are at least three. The command loop assumes Parser.parse either
returns a command or throws, and never returns null.

None of those assumptions is visible at the point that depends on it,
so a later change that breaks one would surface somewhere else as an
IndexOutOfBoundsException or a NullPointerException, if it surfaced at
all.

Let's state each assumption as a Java assert, with a comment saying why
it is expected to hold.

The assertions cover only what the chatbot guarantees itself, never
what the user typed. Bad input is still rejected with a
SallmanException and reported as a reply, because a user making a
typo should not be told the program has a bug. Gradle already enables
assertions for the run task, so they are checked during development
and cost nothing in the released JAR.

commitResults.messageTitle: A-CodeQuality: Remove duplication and split up long methods
commitResults.messageBody:
Reviewing the code against the course's code quality guidelines turns
up three things worth fixing.

The separator between fields in the data file is written out five
times: once in Storage, which reads it, and once each in Task, Todo,
Deadline and Event, which write it. Nothing ties those copies
together, so changing the format means finding all five, and missing
one would leave the reader and the writer quietly disagreeing about
what a saved line looks like.

Storage.parseLine is forty lines working at two levels at once. It
separates the type marker and the done flag from the rest, and it also
knows the field layout of each of the three task types.

Parser.parseDeadline and Parser.parseEvent repeat two shapes eight
times between them: split at a marker and complain if it is missing,
then reject a part the user left empty.

Let's give the separator one definition on Task and have Storage read
it from there, move each task type's field layout into a method of its
own, and replace the repeated checks in the parser with two named
helpers.

Storage now builds its splitting pattern with Pattern.quote rather than
a hand-escaped literal, so the pattern cannot drift from the separator
either. No message the user can see changes, which the text-UI tests
confirm.

commitResults.messageTitle: A-Streams: Replace hand-written loops with streams
commitResults.messageBody:
Several methods build a list or an array by declaring an empty
collection, looping over a source and adding to it as they go. The
mechanics of the loop take up more room than the operation being
performed, and a reader has to follow the accumulator to work out
whether a given loop filters, maps or searches.

TaskList.tasksOn and TaskList.find filter. Storage.save maps each task
to its saved line. CommandType.keywords joins the keywords with commas,
and CommandType.fromKeyword searches for the first match. Ui.sayNumbered
and SallmanException.toLines each build an array from a heading followed
by a sequence.

Let's write each of those as a stream, so that the operation is named
rather than spelled out.

Storage.load keeps its loop. It counts line numbers for its error
messages and catches an exception per line, so that one damaged line
does not stop the rest of the file from loading. A stream expresses
neither of those well.

One behaviour does change: tasksOn and find now return the unmodifiable
list that toList produces, rather than a fresh ArrayList. Nothing
modifies either result, and both are documented as lists to read.

Merge branch 'master' into branch-A-Streams
Merge pull request #2 from SalmanAlfarisi5/branch-A-CodeQuality

Merge pull request #3 from SalmanAlfarisi5/branch-A-Streams

commitResults.messageTitle: A-CI: Check every push with GitHub Actions
commitResults.messageBody:
Nothing checks the project except the person making the change running
./gradlew check by hand. A commit that compiles here can still fail
elsewhere, because the build resolves JavaFX for three platforms while
only one of them is ever exercised locally.

Let's add the GitHub Actions workflow from the course template, which
runs ./gradlew check on Linux, macOS and Windows for every push and
every pull request.

The workflow is the se-edu template unchanged. It validates the Gradle
wrapper before running it, so a tampered wrapper cannot silently run
something else, and it installs a JDK 25 build that bundles JavaFX.
Running check rather than build means the tests and both Checkstyle
tasks have to pass, which is what the parallel branches in this week's
increments needed and could not get automatically.

The README carries the workflow's status badge, so the state of the
default branch is visible without opening the Actions tab.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-CI'
C-Tagging: Let tasks be labelled with tags
commitResults.messageBody:
A task can only be found by the words in its description. Anything that
groups tasks across descriptions, such as which module or which part of
life a task belongs to, has to be written into every description by
hand, and is then indistinguishable from the description itself.

Let's add tags: labels attached to a task with a tag command and taken
off again with untag, shown after the task and searched by find along
with the description.

Tags are stored in lower case so that #Fun and #fun are one label
rather than two, and are restricted to letters, digits, hyphens and
underscores. That keeps a tag free of both whitespace, which separates
one tag from the next, and the field separator, which would make a
saved line ambiguous.

In the data file the tags are one extra field at the end of the line,
marked by a leading #. Being marked rather than merely being last is
what lets a line be read whether it carries dates, tags, both or
neither, and it means a file written before this change still loads: a
line with no # field is simply read as having no tags.

Placing the tags last also meant the task classes could no longer build
their text by wrapping the description from the outside in, since that
put the dates after anything the base class appended. Deadline and
Event now contribute their dates through dateFields and details hooks
instead, leaving Task to assemble the whole line and keep the tags at
the end of it.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-C-Tagging'
C-Undo: Let the last change be undone
commitResults.messageBody:
Every command that changes the list does so immediately and writes the
result to disk. A delete of the wrong task number, or a mark of the
wrong task, can only be put right by working out what the list held
before and typing it back in.

Let's remember the state of the list before each change, and add an
undo command that restores the most recent one.

A state is remembered as copies of the tasks, not as the tasks
themselves. Mark and tag change a task in place while leaving the list
holding the same objects, so a remembered state that shared them would
be changed by the very command it exists to reverse. Task gains a copy
method for this, with each subclass supplying a new instance of its own
type and the base class filling in the done flag and the tags.

The snapshot is taken by each command once it knows it is going to
change something, rather than before it validates its arguments. A
command rejected for a bad task number therefore leaves nothing behind,
and neither does a tag command that only re-adds a tag the task already
had, so undo never spends a step doing nothing visible.

Twenty states are kept. Undo is for walking back over a mistake rather
than over a whole session, and each state holds a copy of every task.
The history lives in memory, so it does not survive a restart; the
error message says as much rather than leaving the user guessing.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-C-Undo'
C-Sort: Let the list be put into a chosen order
commitResults.messageBody:
Tasks stay in the order they were added, which is the order they were
thought of rather than the order they matter in. Finding what is due
next means reading every line and comparing the dates by eye, and the
list only gets harder to read as it grows.

Let's add a sort command that reorders the list, by date, by
description or by whether the task is done.

Sorting by date is what the command is most often wanted for, so a bare
sort does that. A todo carries no date, so it has nothing to be ordered
by; rather than dropping such tasks or floating them to the top, they
are placed last. Task reports the date it should be ordered by as an
Optional, which lets an event be ordered by when it starts without the
comparator having to know which kinds of task carry dates.

The new order is kept rather than being a one-off view: it is saved
like any other change. That also makes it undoable, and since the sort
is stable, tasks the order cannot tell apart stay in the order they
were added, so sorting twice does not shuffle them.

SortOrder is an enum for the same reasons CommandType is one. The
orders are a fixed set the compiler can check, and the message naming
the orders that are understood is built from the constants, so a new
order cannot be added without that message following it.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-C-Sort'
A-MoreErrorHandling: Report each mistake precisely
commitResults.messageBody:
Most bad input is already rejected, but several mistakes are rejected
with a message that is vague or wrong. 2019-02-30 is reported as not
being a date in yyyy-mm-dd form, although it is in that form. A /by
given twice is reported as an unreadable date. An event typed with /to
before /from is told it has no /to. A task number too large for an int
is called "not a number". Other mistakes are not caught at all: the
same task can be added twice, marking a task that is already done
reports success, and repeated spaces are stored as typed.

Let's name each mistake for what it is, and refuse the requests that
would silently change nothing.

- Dates in the right shape that do not exist name the month and how
  many days it has.
- Markers only count as whole words, so a marker joined to a word, a
  marker given twice, and /to before /from each get their own message,
  and a description such as "go /tomorrow" is no longer split at /to.
- Oversized task numbers are reported as outside the list, and more
  than one number is asked to be given one at a time.
- A task matching an existing one, and a mark or unmark that would not
  change the task, are refused before the undo snapshot is taken, so
  they leave no undo step.
- Keywords are matched regardless of case, and a keyword one slip away
  from a command suggests it.
- Runs of spaces in descriptions and search keywords become one space.
- A saved event that ends before it starts is skipped when loading.

Two failures outside the user's control are also handled. An
unexpected exception while running a command is reported as a failed
command instead of ending the session or leaving the GUI without a
reply, and a window layout that cannot be loaded now exits rather than
leaving JavaFX running with nothing on screen.

The existing messages are unchanged apart from the impossible-date
case, whose text-UI test is updated to match.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-MoreErrorHandling'
A-BetterGui: Make the conversation easier to scan
commitResults.messageBody:
The window still shows the tutorial's layout. Both sides of the
conversation get a 99-pixel photo and the same gradient bubble, so on
the default 400-pixel window the pictures take up close to half the
width and long replies wrap into narrow columns. Errors look exactly
like successful replies, so a mistyped command is easy to miss. The
input row is laid out with fixed anchors and an unlabelled text box.

Let's restyle the window around what the user needs to read.

- The two sides are drawn differently, since this is a person talking
  to an app rather than two people talking. The user's messages are
  compact bubbles in the accent colour with no picture. The chatbot's
  replies are plain cards with a small round avatar.
- A reply reporting a problem is tinted red with a thick edge, so it is
  noticed before it is read. The GUI can tell because Sallman now
  reports whether its last reply was an error.
- Bubbles are capped at 80% of the window's width, so a long reply on a
  wide window does not become one very long line.
- The window is a BorderPane, so the conversation takes whatever room
  the window has and the input row stretches with it. The minimum
  width drops to 320 pixels, which the smaller avatar makes usable.
- The input box has placeholder text showing an example command, and
  has focus from the start.

Colours are defined once as named colours on the root, so the look can
be retuned in one place. The user's picture is no longer used and is
removed.

Checked by rendering the real window offscreen at 320, 400 and 900
pixels wide: text wraps within its bubble and nothing is clipped.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-BetterGui'
A-Personality: Give saLLMan an eager AI persona
commitResults.messageBody:
saLLMan's name is already a pun on LLM, but nothing else about it plays
on that. Its replies are the neutral phrasing the project started with,
and the window is a generic chat layout with a stock photo as its
avatar.

Let's give it the personality of an over-eager AI assistant, and carry
that through its wording and its window.

Replies open the way such assistants do. Successes are met with
"Certainly!", "Great job!" or "Great question!". Slips in the user's
input begin "I'm sorry, but" or "I'd love to help, but". Requests that
cannot be met at all, such as a task number past the end of the list
or a date that does not exist, are answered "As a large language
model, I must point out". Undo apologises for any confusion.

The act stays in the opening words. Every task line, count, example
command and hint is unchanged, so a reply still says exactly what
happened. Each tic is used consistently rather than chosen at random,
which keeps the voice recognisable and the tests deterministic. The
replies stay in plain ASCII, since a symbol such as a sparkle can come
out garbled in a console.

The window takes on the same character. A header names saLLMan and
says it is "always eager to help", the avatar becomes a sparkle drawn
for this project in place of the stock photo, and the same sparkle is
the window icon. The colours move to a violet theme, and the input box
reads "Message saLLMan..." above the disclaimer such assistants carry:
"saLLMan can make mistakes."

One behaviour changes. `list` on an empty list used to print a heading
with nothing under it, which reads as though the command half worked.
It now says the list is empty and suggests adding a task.

The text-UI test outputs were regenerated from this build, and a
script confirmed that for every case the number of replies, and the
task lines and numbers in each reply, are the same as before.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-Personality'
A-MoreTesting: Cover nearly all testable code
commitResults.messageBody:
JUnit reaches 76% of the lines and 71% of the branches outside the GUI.
The gaps are not spread evenly. Several commands, including delete,
undo, tag, sort, find and on, are only ever run by the text-UI tests,
and are never checked in isolation. Ui is at 29%, even though a silent
Ui collects its replies so they can be read back. Sallman's console
loop and startup are untested, as are Storage's read and write
failures and its handling of lines with missing fields.

Let's add tests for each of those, and measure the result so the gaps
can be seen rather than guessed at.

- CommandTest runs every command against a real list and a temporary
  data file, checking what changed, what was said and what was saved.
- UiTest checks the wording of every reply, including both empty and
  non-empty lists, and how the console is printed to and read from.
- SallmanTest drives the console loop with prepared input, covering
  blank lines, errors, stopping at bye and input that ends without it.
- StorageTest makes reading and saving fail for real, by putting a
  folder where the data file should be and a file where its folder
  should be.

Coverage outside the GUI is now 98.8% of lines and 95.5% of branches.
What remains is listed in test/manual-testing.md with the reason for
each part: assertion failures and last-resort handlers that only a bug
can reach, and paths that would write to the real task list.

Writing the tests turned up one bug. A single skipped line was reported
as "so I skipped them"; the wording now agrees with the count.

JaCoCo is added to the build, so ./gradlew jacocoTestReport produces the
same report, and CI publishes it on every push. The manual-testing page
records the checks automated tests cannot make: the CI-built JAR
opening on Windows 11 and on Ubuntu, and the window drawn at its
minimum, default and a wide size.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-Acknowledgements'
Show dates and match text the same in every locale
commitResults.messageBody:
Dates are shown with the month abbreviated in the computer's own
language. On a computer set to British or Singapore English, September
is written "Sept" rather than "Sep"; German writes "Sept."; Chinese
uses characters. None of the tests noticed, because every date they use
falls in October, which is "Oct" in all forms of English.

Tags, search and sorting by name have the same flaw in a less visible
place: they lower-case text using the computer's language rules. On a
computer set to Turkish, a capital I lower-cases to a dotless i, so a
tag typed as WISHLIST would no longer match wishlist.

Let's format dates with English month names and lower-case text with
language-neutral rules, so saLLMan behaves the same whatever language
the computer is set to.

The new tests switch the default locale while they run. Each was
confirmed to fail with its fix reverted: showing September on this
computer, which is set to Singapore English, produced "Sept".

to a first command. A short section then explains the conventions every
command shares, so each command's own section can stay brief: its
format, an example, and only the rules a user would otherwise trip
over. It ends with a summary table.

chatbot, and the sample task line matches its real output exactly.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-UserGuide'
Keep descriptions that look like tags intact
commitResults.messageBody:
A task's tags are saved as a last field on its line, marked with a
leading #, and are left out entirely when the task has none. For an
untagged todo, the description is therefore the last field. A todo
described as "buy milk | #urgent" is saved as

    T | 0 | buy milk | #urgent

and read back as "buy milk" tagged urgent. "pack bag | #" loses its
ending altogether. Nothing warns the user; the text simply changes
after a restart.

Let's write an empty tag field whenever an untagged task's last field
would otherwise start with #, so such a line is saved as

    T | 0 | buy milk | #urgent | #

and the empty field is what gets read as the tags.

Every other line is saved exactly as before. A tagged task already ends
in its real tag field, and a deadline or event ends in a date, so the
extra field is needed only by untagged todos whose descriptions end
this way. Files written before this change load as they always did.

The new tests were written first and failed against the old code. Two
more pin down the lines that must not change: a tagged task, and a
deadline whose description looks like tags.

Found by a code review from OpenAI Codex.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Document the window setup and one-day events
commitResults.messageBody:

more than its inherited description says: it sets the window's title,
icon and minimum size, connects the chatbot, and shuts JavaFX down if
the layout cannot be loaded.

The parser also accepts an event that starts and ends on the same date
without saying why. A reader could take that for a missed check, since
start dates equal to end dates are a common thing to reject.

Let's describe what Main.start does, and note beside the date check
that events are recorded in whole days, so a same-date event lasts one
day rather than no time at all, and rejecting it would leave no way to
record a one-day event.

Honour a named data file in the GUI too
commitResults.messageBody:
The README says a different data file can be used by naming it when
starting saLLMan, as in ./gradlew run --args="path/to/tasks.txt". That
stopped working when the GUI became the main entry point. Gradle now
starts the GUI, which always uses data/sallman.txt; only the console
version still reads the argument. Naming a file is silently ignored,
and saLLMan reads and changes the default file instead.

Sallman.dataPathFrom takes the command-line arguments and returns the
first one, or the default file when there are none. The console's main
method and the GUI's Main both use it, the GUI reading the arguments
JavaFX was started with.

commitResults.messageTitle: Refuse extra words after list, undo and bye
commitResults.messageBody:
list, undo and bye take nothing after their keyword, but anything typed
there is silently ignored. That is not always harmless. "undo twice"
undoes once, without saying the rest was ignored, and "bye later" exits
straight away.

Let's refuse input after these three commands, naming the command and
showing its correct form, as the other commands already do for input
they cannot use. A refusal changes nothing, so it leaves no undo step.

The new test was written first and failed against the old code, and a
text-UI case checks that each refusal leaves the list as it was.

commitResults.messageTitle: Check tags read from the data file
commitResults.messageBody:
A typed tag must be letters, digits, hyphens and underscores, but tags
read back from the data file are not checked at all. A hand-edited
line such as "T | 0 | buy milk | #bad!tag" loads with that tag, which
then can never be removed: untag refuses the same name as invalid.

Let's check saved tags against the same rule as typed ones, and skip a
line holding an invalid tag, reporting why, as the loader already does
for other lines it cannot use.

The rule moves from Parser to Task.isValidTag, so typing a tag and
loading one cannot drift apart. The real app now reports such a line
when it starts, and loads the rest of the file.

Found by a code review from OpenAI Codex.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Describe how sorting treats ties accurately
commitResults.messageBody:
The User Guide and TaskList say that tasks a sort cannot tell apart
stay in the order they were added. The sort is stable, which keeps
such tasks in the order they are in at the time, and since a sort is
saved, that can be the order of an earlier sort rather than the order
they were added. Sorting by status after sorting by name keeps each
group in name order, not in the order the tasks were added.

Let's describe ties as keeping their current order, with that example
in the guide, and fix the field comment in TaskList that said the list
is always in the order tasks were added.

Checked on the running app with tasks added out of name order.

Found by a code review from OpenAI Codex.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Use American spelling and plural collection names
commitResults.messageBody:
The coding standard asks for names and comments in American spelling,
and for names of collections to be plural. Checkstyle cannot check
either, and a few places miss both. A method is named colourByCommand,
comments say "recognised", "recognisably", "pluralised" and "coloured",
and three collections have singular names: the lines of a reply in Ui,
the tasks restored by undo in TaskList, and the fields of a saved line
in Storage.

Let's rename the method to colorByCommand, use American spelling in
those comments and the stylesheets' comments, and call the collections
replyLines, previousTasks and fields.

Only names and comments change. The chatbot's own words, such as "I
apologise", are part of its personality and stay as they are.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-final-review'
Keep saved tasks safe when the file cannot be read
commitResults.messageBody:
The data file is read as strict UTF-8, all at once. One byte that is not
valid UTF-8 makes the whole file unreadable. That is easy to cause: an
accented letter saved by an editor using a Windows code page is enough.
saLLMan then starts with an empty list, but still saves to the same
file, so the next change replaces every task in it. Adding one todo to
a three-task file with "cafe" spelled with an accent left the file
holding only the new todo.

Let's fix this in two layers.

- Decode the file line by line. A line that is not valid UTF-8 is
  skipped and reported, as other damaged lines already are, and the
  rest of the file loads. A byte order mark at the start of the file,
  which some Windows editors write, is ignored rather than making the
  first task unreadable, which it also used to.
- If the file still cannot be read at all, refuse to save over it for
  the rest of the session, and say why, so its contents stay intact
  until the user fixes or moves it.

The User Guide describes both. The new tests were written first and all
four failed against the old code, including one that reproduces the
data loss end to end.

Found by a code review from OpenAI Codex.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Leave undo history alone when sort changes nothing
commitResults.messageBody:
Every sort records an undo step and saves the list, even when the list
is already in the order asked for. Undo after such a sort then appears
to do nothing, because it restores an identical list. Twenty unchanged
sorts push real changes out of the undo history, although the User
Guide promises the last twenty changes can be undone. Mark and tag
already avoid this by leaving no step when nothing would change.

Let's check whether the list is already in the requested order before
sorting. If it is, the list is shown as usual but not saved, and no
undo step is recorded. Since the sort is stable, tasks the order cannot
separate count as already in order.

On the running app, "todo read book", then "sort", then "undo" now
removes the task, rather than restoring the list unchanged.

Found by a code review from OpenAI Codex.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Number find and on results by list position
commitResults.messageBody:

a task's position in the whole list. The two sets of numbers disagree
whenever a result is not also at the top of the list. After "todo read
book", "todo buy bread" and "find bread", the result is shown as "1.",
and "delete 1" then removes "read book" instead.

Let's show each result with its position in the whole list, so the
number next to a task found by a search is the number to type to act
on it. Positions are found by identity, so of two identical tasks from
an older data file the right one is numbered.

The User Guide now says find and on show those numbers, and the
text-UI test plan's find case describes the new numbering. A script
regenerated the plan's expected output and confirmed that the only
replies to change were three find and on replies, showing the same
tasks with different numbers. A new test finds a task and deletes it
by the number shown.
